title: AGNTCon + MCPCon 2026: Agentic AI Foundation Adds Four Projects as MCP Turns to Security
summary:
At AGNTCon + MCPCon North America 2026, the Agentic AI Foundation added OpenSandbox, Open Responses, Agent Skills, and OpenEnv, reaching ten projects in its first year. Keynotes from Anthropic, OpenAI, Google, and UC Berkeley focused on MCP in production, security, and agents with their own identities.

By Andrew Hoblitzell

Lily Mara explains how to avoid high-risk software rewrites through incremental FFI refactoring. She shares how engineering teams can replace Python bottlenecks with Rust via PyO3, demonstrating how to achieve dramatic function-level speedups, seamless integration testing, and meaningful infrastructure cost savings without microservice overhead. Agentic LLM systems have moved from linear prompt chains to graph-based workflows and, more recently, code-executing harnesses. Chains are simple but fragile, graphs add branching, retries, and validation, and code harnesses verify outputs through execution. The article advises validating model outputs and choosing the least complex design that meets reliability, speed, and cost needs. Manju Rajashekhar explains how the actor model solves the complex runtime challenges of production AI agents. By treating agents as distributed systems, he discusses state ownership, message passing, write-through state, and supervision boundaries to manage failures, continuations, and mutable execution graphs, moving agentic workflows beyond fragile demos to resilient architecture. Nathen Harvey shares insights from DORA research on AI adoption in software delivery. He explains why AI acts as an amplifier, how the DORA AI Capabilities Model drives outcomes, and why engineering leaders must evolve beyond bottlenecks like code reviews to achieve sustainable productivity, reduce delivery instability, and empower developers without burning out their teams. Andrew Martin discusses why AI security is fundamentally tied to Kubernetes security. He shares insights into the evolving AI threat landscape, covering non-deterministic agent behavior, GPU supply chain vulnerabilities, shared compute risks, and practical defense strategies - from prompt firewalling to agentic identity - to help secure cloud-native AI workloads in production environments. title: Scale agents securely with IAM Helper Agent Skills and MCP Tools
summary:
As organizations adopt autonomous agents to build applications, securing identities and access has become more challenging. Developers relying on agents to provision cloud resources, write Terraform, and deploy microservices at machine-speed only find their CI/CD pipelines blocked even faster as security friction scales.  

To help you get ahead of agentic-era Identity and Access Management, today we’re introducing IAM Helper. This suite of intelligent, agent-facing building blocks can automate complex, end-to-end IAM workflows. 

As an agent-native orchestration and interface layer for Google Cloud IAM, it augments Google Cloud’s core IAM engines — including Policy Intelligence and Privileged Access Manager (PAM) — making IAM skills callable directly by autonomous code assistants, deployment pipelines, and custom agents. Using this functionality reduces the administrative overhead of maintaining least-privilege security and agent governance, while maximizing utility, and accelerating deployment.

IAM Helper Agent Skills: Fast, secure deployment with automated governance

Manual troubleshooting of permission blockers creates friction for engineering and administrators, while shortcuts can lead to broad agent over-permissioning that puts least privilege at risk. 

IAM Helper empowers agents to handle access management dynamically. It shifts the burden of policy evaluation away from human administrators and LLMs, offloading complex orchestration directly to the Google Cloud backend, to maximize token efficiency and prevent costly operational bottlenecks.

Rather than operating as isolated utilities, IAM Helper Agent Skills guide agents through the cloud access lifecycle. These end-to-end workflows, helper scripts, and guardrails packaged using the open Agent Skills standard can orchestrate multiple underlying functions and APIs to resolve complex IAM tasks. They work across common agents (Gemini CLI, Gemini Cloud Assist, ADK, Claude Code, and Cursor). 

Built-in guardrails and real-world impact

Every IAM Helper agent skill separates read-only discovery from policy changes: Diagnostics and simulations run automatically, while any change to access policies pauses for human-in-the-loop (HITL) confirmation based on customizable risk tiers. To see the value of IAM Helper in practice, consider how it transforms two everyday scenarios:

  • Scaled user-assisted remediation: Suppose a developer's coding agent hits a 403 error while deploying a new application. Rather than filing a support ticket and idling, the agent uses iam-helper-for-troubleshooting to identify the missing Pub/Sub permission in seconds, then uses iam-helper-for-privileged-access-management to request a one-hour JIT grant, eliminating hours of debugging friction.

  • Autonomous pipeline self-healing: An infrastructure agent encounters a permission block during a routine deployment pipeline. Rather than failing the build, the pipeline uses IAM Helper Agent skills to generate a revised, least-privilege policy, verifies against 90 days of logs via iam-helper-for-policy-simulator that active services won't break, and routes the change to an admin for quick approval.

IAM Helper Agent Skills are designed for maximum token and cost efficiency, allowing agents to execute multi-step administrative operations autonomously.

  1. Authoring compliant, least-privilege policies: As DevOps engineers translate access requirements into JSON, YAML, or Terraform HCL, iam-helper-for-policy-management generates and validates IAM v1 allow bindings and IAM v2 deny rules. It automatically catches and blocks risky configs before they are applied, including public access (allUsers) and broad basic roles (roles/owner, roles/editor).

  2. Unblocking 403 errors in seconds: When an on-call engineer or deployment agent hits a cryptic 403 PERMISSION_DENIED error, iam-helper-for-troubleshooting identifies the exact missing permission or blocking rule in seconds. It adapts to the user’s role: Developers can check if they can unblock themselves locally or generate a structured ticket for their administrator (Requester flow), while security administrators can trace inherited allow and v2 deny rules across organization, folder, and project hierarchies to resolve the issue (Resolver flow).

  3. Simulating blast radius before rolling out changes: Before a platform engineer updates a policy or applies IAM Recommender role reductions, they need confidence that active workloads won't break. iam-helper-for-policy-simulator walks the agent through a structured plan, simulate, analyze, and apply flow, testing proposed changes against 90 days of historical access logs to confirm existing traffic won't be disrupted before any update takes effect.

  4. Elevating access just-in-time instead of granting standing privileges: When responders or maintenance agents need temporary production access, iam-helper-for-privileged-access-management manages the lifecycle of on-demand credentials through Privileged Access Manager (PAM). It supports requester, administrator, and approver workflows so elevated access is audited, time-bound, and automatically revoked once the task is done.

While IAM Helper Agent Skills supply the high-level workflow logic, they are all based on a common set of foundational MCP Tools. 

Powered by Google Cloud IAM MCP tools

Google Cloud IAM Helper MCP tools provide the backend connection through atomic, read-only functions exposed via Google-managed MCP servers across core IAM endpoints (Policy Troubleshooter, Policy Analyzer, Policy Simulator, and IAM v1/v2 APIs). 

Rather than requiring teams to write custom API wrappers, MCP tools give agents a standard way to query the cloud backend and get exact answers without parsing verbose policy documents in the prompt, maximizing token efficiency. Agents can dynamically discover and invoke these tools to execute basic operations like checking permissions or listing roles when custom logic is required.

Because operations like hierarchy traversal, group expansion, and policy evaluation happen on dedicated IAM endpoints (spanning IAM v1 allow roles, IAM v2 deny, Policy Troubleshooter, and Policy Analyzer), skills run quickly and accurately with minimal token usage. Teams can also use these atomic MCP tools directly when writing their own custom Agent Skills, making it straightforward to combine Google Cloud's IAM capabilities with internal ticketing systems, custom compliance checks, and existing deployment pipelines.

Getting started

Accelerate your agentic workflows, reduce operational overhead, and bring intelligent, scalable security to your deployment pipelines. Start building with IAM Helper Agent skills today by exploring our Google Cloud Agent Skills Catalog and dive deeper with the official IAM documentation.

title: Cross-request KV cache exposure in the GLM-5.3 Workers AI model, and our remediation with SGLang
summary: A configuration mismatch in GLM 5.3 on Workers AI triggered an SGLang bug that exposed KV cache pages across requests. Here is how we addressed the issue.
story_key: model:glm|ver:5.3|title:cross request kv cache exposure in the glm 5 3 workers ai model and our remediat
content_excerpt: On September 8, 2026, we were alerted by a security researcher, Gadi Evron from Knostic, to a tenant isolation issue affecting the GLM-5.3 Workers AI model ( @cf/zai-org/glm-5.3 ) starting on August 27, 2026. We have remediated the issue, and we restored the model on September 9. We have confirmed that no other model hosted on Workers AI was affected. Between August 27 and September 9, a small number of customers using the GLM 5.3 Workers AI model received responses that contained data from other customers' requests made to the same model shortly before theirs. In total, 155 responses were affected, all to prompts longer than 681,280 tokens. After excluding our own testing and the researcher's, the requests we identified are consistent in timing and volume with ordinary long-context use, not with someone repeatedly exploiting the bug. We found no evidence of deliberate exploitation. Today we are publishing this report alongside a post from SGLang, the open-source inference engine that we use, as a coordinated disclosure. This post describes the bug that caused this issue, our response timeline, and the subsequent hardening we have conducted on our production SGLang deployments. We also detail our continued efforts with the upstream maintainers of SGLang to address this and similar bugs. GLM is a text generation model from Z.ai that is built for agentic coding workflows; it is one of the many models available through Workers AI. Gadi Evron submitted a report on September 8 through our HackerOne program stating that very long prompts sent to @cf/zai-org/glm-5.3 on Workers AI sometimes returned text that belonged to other users' sessions. Cloudflare reproduced the issue the next morning and took the model offline within 40 minutes of declaring an incident. We then deployed a corrected configuration and a patched inference engine, and restored service the same day. This specific report of cross-request KV cache exposure was the result of two overlapping issues. The first was a misconfiguration of the open-source inference engine, SGLang, used by Cloudflare. We deployed GLM 5.3 with a 1,048,576-token context window, but the KV cache pool on our prefill GPUs only had room for 681,280 tokens. We were aware of this mismatch before launch. We expected the engine to return an error for any prompt it could not process, and our long-context tests returned successful responses, so we did not believe this to be an issue. The second was a bug in how SGLang handled the re

title: claude-code v2.1.311
summary:
What's changed

  • Added --hold-idle-file and --max-hold-min to self-hosted-runner, to keep an idle session while your host reports processes it left running
  • Added a tip for the Explanatory output style, shown when you ask Claude for explanations
  • Fixed long freezes at startup and after reading or editing files when a CLAUDE.md file holds a very long list item
  • Fixed interrupting Claude not taking effect until a timeout while an MCP server had not answered a resource read or a skill was still downloading
  • Fixed standard-context sessions stopping with "Usage credits required for 1M context" when a request ran over 200K tokens; Claude Code now compacts the conversation and continues
  • Fixed Write and Edit stalling for up to 5 seconds after they ran, and reporting 0 lines changed, when changing thousands of lines in a file
  • Fixed subagents being unable to use MCP tools from servers that finish connecting after the subagent starts
  • Fixed Claude seeing stale MEMORY.md and CLAUDE.md content right after automatic compaction when those files were edited earlier in the session
  • Fixed claude -p and SDK sessions saving transcript messages out of order or keeping messages that were taken back
  • Fixed SubagentStop hooks running about twice a minute for each running subagent instead of once when it finishes
  • Fixed the @ file picker ignoring .ignore/.rgignore negation rules that re-include git-ignored files
  • Fixed a subagent's isolated worktree being removed while a background subagent it started was still working in it
  • Fixed background agents in auto mode that wait on their own shells starting a new main conversation turn on every wake
  • Fixed the Bash tool description claiming the working directory always persists between calls
  • Fixed the environment block naming a shell commands don't run in, such as fish when the Bash tool uses zsh
  • Fixed claude mcp add, claude mcp remove and /mcp naming the current folder instead of the project entry in ~/.claude.json that holds a local-scope server when run below a repository root
  • Fixed claude mcp list and claude mcp get showing the error code twice on failed-connection lines (for example ENOENT: ENOENT: …)
  • Fixed Remote Control sessions staying on "Connecting" for about two minutes when a network proxy blocks a startup request
  • Fixed messages that Claude sends to a cloud or Remote Control session appearing as your own message in the Claude mobile apps
  • Fixed Claude not being told the cause when a file attached to a message sent over Remote Control or to a cloud session could not be saved because the disk was full, or that a message's attachments past the first 20 were left out
  • Fixed WebFetch and WebSearch hanging on a stalled response in Cowork cloud sessions; an unfinished request now fails after 300 seconds
  • Fixed a background session that crashed between turns not being restarted while it was attached, pinned, or had a scheduled task or wake-up set
  • Fixed the "background service did not respond" error suggesting the disabled claude daemon restart; it now suggests claude daemon stop --any and says it ends background sessions
  • Fixed claude respawn <id> starting the background service before reporting that no background session matches the id
  • Fixed /effort not warning about a prompt cache miss in plan mode when the plan model differs from the session model
  • Fixed /ide saying the VS Code extension was installed before the install finished or when it failed
  • Fixed the Write tool's file preview skipping rows and miscounting hidden lines when a line is wider than the terminal
  • Fixed ↑ in an agent's chat tab recalling a message that was still waiting to be delivered, so resending it sent a second copy
  • Fixed Cowork cloud sessions losing their connectors and most tools after a restart when a plugin or your settings named an agent; Cowork cloud sessions now ignore that setting
  • Fixed agent teams sessions showing an empty task list when coming back with --resume, --continue, /resume or --session-id, including after /clear or a crash, and /branch writing to the original session's list
  • Fixed pasting text that mentions an image file, such as ! open /tmp/shot.png or /review look at /tmp/shot.png, attaching the image and dropping its path from the prompt
  • Fixed the feedback draft card showing its 1/2/0 and Esc shortcuts while the prompt has text, when those keys act on the prompt instead of the card
  • Fixed a lone backslash in quotes or brackets, like "\" or (\), disappearing from Claude's responses
  • Fixed agent teammates compacting their history when DISABLE_COMPACT is set
  • Fixed the rewind menu offering "Summarize from here" and "Summarize up to here" when DISABLE_COMPACT is set
  • Fixed a finished /code-review, or another skill that runs in a sub-agent, running a second time when a cloud or background session restarts
  • Fixed long hidden thinking being cut off as idle on Google Vertex AI, Microsoft Foundry and Claude Platform on AWS, where the endpoint sends thinking progress updates
  • Fixed /ide saying it had installed the JetBrains plugin when nothing was installed
  • Fixed Claude Pro and Max subscribers being told to ask their admin when their subscription can't be used; the message now points to billing settings
  • Fixed the diff pane opening by itself after an edit in wide fullscreen terminals when it had nothing to show
  • Fixed /mcp showing a remote server as failed after "Clear authentication" when the server works without sign-in
  • Fixed /mcp showing "authenticated" for a remote server that Claude Code sends no credentials to
  • Fixed a --plugin-dir folder of plugins loading as one plugin when an empty .mcp.json was at its top
  • Fixed /usage never showing large prompt-cache misses under "What's contributing to your limits usage?"
  • Fixed status line links staying plain text in background sessions after you open them from a terminal that supports links
  • Fixed the /rewind confirmation saying the conversation "will be forked" when the later messages are removed from the conversation
  • Fixed the /rewind warning that wrongly said manual and Bash edits are never affected by a code restore
  • Fixed plan approval in screen reader mode sending feedback you had dismissed with Escape
  • Fixed Claude Code retrying requests the API marked not to retry, which could hold a turn for minutes or, in unattended retry mode (CLAUDE_CODE_RETRY_WATCHDOG), indefinitely
  • Linux: Fixed sandboxed Bash commands failing with bwrap: Can't create file when a --plugin-dir folder was also an added directory and permissions.blockReadsOutsideWorkingDirectories was on
  • Self-hosted runner: Fixed a session failing to start when a rate limit (HTTP 429, or a git wrapper that exits 75) blocks an added read-only repository; it now starts without that repository
  • Improved startup time for Pro and Max accounts by skipping two network requests on launches within an hour of the last check
  • Improved /teleport and claude --teleport to warn when a compacted cloud session loads from its last compaction, so the messages it summarized aren't in the local copy
  • Improved the messages shown when a background session's process exits: they no longer promise a restart that isn't coming, and they say how to resume the session
  • Improved artifacts with several views: Claude now routes each view on the link's #name and no longer says the address bar stays the same as you switch views
  • Improved shell commands that reach their timeout: the result now shows the output so far and says the command is still running in the background
  • Improved compaction: when the model's reply has no summary in it, Claude Code now usually asks for the summary once more before it replaces the conversation
  • Improved the Artifact tool's choice between a page and a document: explainers and visual or interactive work become artifact pages; documents are for writing people keep editing or pass around
  • Improved startup time for launches whose only arguments are options and their values, such as claude --model opus
  • Improved the "Connection dropped" API error: it now says where to look first (the proxy or gateway in use, else VPN or firewall; Anthropic API only, Bedrock, Vertex and Foundry are unchanged)
  • Improved screen reader mode: deleting a rule in /permissions says "Deleted allow rule …" right away
  • Improved the message shown when a pasted sign-in code is refused: it now says the code may have expired or been used, and to sign in again
  • Improved Slack connector sends: Claude now checks a channel's topic for posting rules before messaging a channel you didn't name
  • Improved screen reader mode: Claude's questions are listed as "Questions: Color (answered), Pages", without arrows or symbols
  • Changed ultrathink in the interactive terminal to run its turn at xhigh effort on Opus 5.5, Sonnet 5.5, Haiku 5.5 and Fable 5.1 through Anthropic's API; typed while Claude is working, it raises the rest of that turn
  • Changed the ultrathink rainbow to appear only where the keyword can raise effort, and not when the word is quoted or part of a file path
  • Changed Ctrl+D in agent view to match the prompt: on an empty input, pressing it twice exits
  • Changed --output-format json and stream-json output to write DEL, C1 control and Unicode format characters inside strings as \uXXXX escapes; parsed values are unchanged
  • Changed model names and IDs to drop the [1m] suffix and its label on models where the suffix has no effect; the suffix is still accepted
  • Changed startup warnings about permission rules in settings files to show once per user until the rule changes
  • Changed /code-review to tell Claude to put the effort level first and use max only when asked
  • Changed DISABLE_COMPACT in settings files and in a mod's $.env.set so they can only turn compaction off, not back on
  • Changed Claude Code on Bedrock, Mantle, Vertex, and Foundry to load model settings from a signed file on downloads.claude.ai; set CLAUDE_CODE_MODEL_CATALOG=off to turn this off
  • Changed sessions that set CLAUDE_CODE_SYNC_SKILLS with feature-flag fetching off to reuse a claude.ai skills list up to 10 minutes old that another session on the machine fetched
  • Changed clicks on scrollbar arrows and bars in fullscreen lists to act when the mouse button is released, so moving off the scrollbar before letting go cancels the click
  • Changed claude purge to say it deletes data only on this computer, not anything stored by Anthropic
  • [VSCode] Added syntax coloring to code blocks in Claude's replies, in light, dark and high contrast dark themes
  • [VSCode] Added a "Running UserPromptSubmit hooks" spinner status and screen reader announcement for slow UserPromptSubmit hooks
  • [VSCode] Fixed custom skills and custom slash commands sent from the VS Code or JetBrains panel leaving out the open file or selected lines that ordinary messages include (#102799)
  • [VSCode] Fixed the extension host freezing while the login shell ran its start-up files to read PATH on macOS and Linux
  • [VSCode] Fixed clicking an image in a tool result, or closing its preview, also opening the result's text in an editor tab
  • [VSCode] Fixed voice dictation continuing to record after a message was sent with the Send button; sending now stops dictation first, as pressing Enter already did
  • [VSCode] Changed the extension to start Claude Code sessions with DISABLE_TELEMETRY set while VS Code's telemetry setting is off, so they send no usage metrics or error reports and fetch no feature flags
  • [VSCode] Changed the session list side bar to load Web sessions when the Web tab is first opened, not at startup
  • [Cloud sessions] Fixed routines in Anthropic-hosted environments staying locked after their owner left the organization and rejoined; the owner can now turn them back on
  • [Cloud sessions] Fixed a failed routine API token delete or regenerate showing nothing if the edit dialog had already closed; it now shows an error toast
  • [Cloud sessions] Fixed cloud environment dialogs, including the admin dialog, accepting duplicate names; they now refuse a name another listed environment already has
  • [Claude Tag] Added a Skills view to Claude Tag analytics showing how often Claude runs each attached skill in Slack channels and which go unused, with Usage links in admin settings
  • [Claude Tag] Improved Claude Tag routines that run in a new session: a run with nothing to report can now end without posting a throwaway message to the channel
  • [Claude Tag] Changed Claude Tag admin settings to show a lock instead of # for private Slack channels that your own Slack account can see
  • [Code Review] Improved Code Review's check run to say no further automatic review will start when the model still can't analyze a change on the automatic retry
  • [Code Review] Improved Code Review reliability: a review whose session fails to start because of a transient server fault is now retried once automatically, and its check run says so

title: Building live intelligence: Databricks AI Search supports Streaming Tables, Materialized Views, and Managed tables using Iceberg
summary: AI Search now natively supports Streaming Tables, Materialized Views, and Managed...
story_key: story|title:building live intelligence databricks ai search supports streaming tables materi
content_excerpt: AI Search now natively supports Streaming Tables, Materialized Views, and Managed tables using Iceberg v3+ in addition to Delta tables. You can bring live events, continuously maintained personalized state, and open-format data directly into your AI Search applications — reducing the overhead of building and managing separate pipelines to convert and synchronize these data sources. Streaming Tables, Materialized Views, and Managed Iceberg each represent a different way of working with data, and each opens up new possibilities for AI applications. Continuously changing data such as new listings, inventory, availability, and user activity can flow into an append-only Streaming Table, with AI Search indexing new records as they arrive and keeping the search index up to date. This freshness enables applications where the latest data can directly shape the search experience: helping users discover newly available restaurants through a search bar, or generating real-time recommendations based on recent trends. Materialized Views can aggregate events, filter records, and join data from multiple sources to create customized state. As the underlying data changes, the view is incrementally maintained and AI Search propagates those changes to the index, enabling personalized search experiences such as session-aware recommendations, product and content discovery based on recent activity, or tailor results to a user's evolving interests and preferences. Managed Iceberg tables can serve as AI Search sources directly, without conversion or migration to another table format, making open-format data available to search indexes and other AI applications. The open-format enables AI applications that work across existing data environments: search across product catalogs managed by different systems, unify business or customer data stored across Managed Iceberg tables, or build search experiences over large, distributed datasets without moving the underlying data. Before native support, customers had to create a separate Delta representation of Streaming Tables, Materialized Views, or Managed Iceberg tables and build pipelines to keep it synchronized with the source. This added an extra data layer, custom update logic, and ongoing operational overhead. Now, AI Search connects directly to these sources. title: vLLM Delivers Day-0 Support for MiniMax-M3.1-Flash
summary: Day-0 vLLM support for MiniMax-M3.1-Flash on NVIDIA Blackwell, NVIDIA Rubin, and AMD MI350-series GPUs, with NVFP4 MSA kernels, NVFP4 MegaMoE, DSpark speculative decoding, AgentX results, and day-0 RL.
story_key: model:vllm|ver:3.1|variant:flash|title:vllm delivers day 0 support for minimax m3 1 flash
content_excerpt: MiniMax-M3.1-Flash is the latest model in the MiniMax-M3 family, with improvements across reasoning, coding, agentic, and visual tasks. It is also built for inference efficiency, with a native NVFP4 KV cache, NVFP4-quantized MoE weights, and a DSpark draft model for speculative decoding. vLLM supports MiniMax-M3.1-Flash on day 0 on NVIDIA Blackwell GPUs, on NVIDIA Rubin GPUs with dedicated Rubin kernels, and on AMD MI350-series GPUs, with strong performance on agentic workloads. Note that the model will only be available in the nightly PyPI wheel after the code is reviewed and merged upstream, which usually takes about a week. Full recipes are at vLLM Recipes , and the checkpoint is at MiniMaxAI/MiniMax-M3.1-Flash . The MiniMax-M3 model family replaces full attention with a variant of block-sparse attention ( arXiv 2606.13392 ) to make inference more efficient. The KV cache is split into blocks of 128 tokens. A lightweight indexer scores every key in the context with one index query per GQA group against a single shared index-key head, then max-pools those scores into one score per block. Main attention then runs exactly, but only over the top 16 blocks, and the most recent block is always kept. That caps each query at 2,048 keys, however long the context is. The payoff is largest in decode, which is limited by memory bandwidth. Each step still scans the index keys for the whole context, but that is only 128 bytes per token per layer, an eighth of the 1,024 bytes of K/V that dense attention would read (FP8, 4 KV heads × 128 dims). The full K/V is then read for just the 2,048 selected tokens. At long-context decode, per-step HBM traffic drops to about 12.5% of what dense attention reads. Figure 1: MiniMax Sparse Attention. Each GQA group's indexer picks its top KV blocks, and every query head in that group attends exactly over only those blocks. Step through it. MiniMax-M3.1 greatly improves inference efficiency over the previous generation: it was natively quantization-aware trained for an NVFP4 KV cache, and its routed MoE weights are stored in NVFP4. The NVFP4 experts shrink the checkpoint from 451.5 GB (MiniMax-M3-MXFP8) to 250.1 GB, which is 44.6% smaller. The NVFP4 KV cache needs 34,560 bytes per token instead of 61,440 bytes in FP8, a saving of 43.75% per token. Together, on four NVIDIA B300 GPUs with DEP4 deployment and 256K-token sequences, M3.1 fits 76 concurrent sequences where M3 with an FP8 KV cache fits 28, about 2.7× as many on the same hardw

title: Automating Feature Flag Cleanup at Scale with Multi-Agent LLM Systems: An Industrial Experience at DoorDash
summary: Feature flags are runtime configuration mechanisms used for gradual feature rollouts, experimentation, and kill switches. Once a feature is fully rolled out, the flag and its gated code become technical debt and can introduce operational risk through inadvertently enabling dormant code paths. At DoorDash, over 56,000 feature flags span 623 repositories, with 1,659 currently stale as of May 2026, with internal estimates of one to two hours per manual cleanup. Existing rule-based cleanup tools proved insufficient in DoorDash's codebases. Our contribution is an end-to-end automated LLM-based feature flag cleanup system that integrates querying live feature flag rollout data using MCP, Jira ticket processing, and end-to-end pull request creation. Our system successfully produced engineer-approved flag removal PRs for 45 (90%) of the 50 stale flags it was evaluated on, proving the system's operational viability at scale with each cleanup averaging only $4.79 and 13.8 minutes. We evaluated the system's quality and reliability boundary based on success rates, cost per cleanup and time metrics. Furthermore, we discuss our lessons learned when architecting this system, to provide practical guidance for developing similar multi-agent systems.

title: Multi-Tool Selection for Robotic Systems: Comparing Semantic Retrieval and LLM
summary: Natural-language interfaces allow users to command robotic systems without interacting directly with mission planners or robotics middleware. Their reliable use depends on robot tool routing, defined here as the selection of the smallest complete subset of predefined executable capabilities required to satisfy a request. This task is particularly difficult for compound instructions, where incomplete selection may omit necessary sensing or monitoring capabilities, while excessive selection may expose irrelevant tools. We compare four routing strategies: three progressively refined ChromaDB-based methods - fixed-threshold retrieval, relative-distance retrieval, and clause-aware aggregated retrieval - and a cloud-hosted 120-billion-parameter language-model baseline. The methods are evaluated on 164 manually annotated prompts organised into three complexity levels, from direct single-tool requests to compound requests requiring at least three tools. Using exact-match accuracy, completeness, precision, a completeness-weighted composite score, and routing latency, CDB-v3 achieves the best macro-average score among the retrieval-only methods, with 0.7822, compared with 0.8869 for the large-model baseline. Although the LLM provides higher routing quality, CDB-v3 exhibits substantially lower latency and can be deployed locally without requiring cloud connectivity. These results identify a quality-latency trade-off between direct large-model selection and clause-aware semantic retrieval for privacy-sensitive, connectivity-constrained, and resource-constrained robotic systems.

title: The five components of building a "company harness"
summary: Learn how LangChain built internal agents across marketing, sales, and engineering, and how they have completely changed how those teams work.
story_key: story|title:the five components of building a company harness
content_excerpt: We've built internal agents at LangChain across marketing, sales, and engineering, and they have completely changed how those teams work. They weren't easy to get right. We spent a lot of time solving the problems that come with a multiplayer harness, and every team landed on the same core primitives: To ground this discussion, a brief overview of the three main agents we have at LangChain: GTM Agent : a proactive, always-on agent that assists with GTM activities. Monitors and responds to emails, to new qualified leads, sends daily briefs, can answer questions about accounts, can run outbound motions OpenSWE : our engineering agent, can work on and draft PRs, but also runs code review over all PRs Content Studio : our marketing agent, can draft assets (blogs, images, PowerPoints, videos) in our style and with knowledge of our positioning All of these agents are built in the same way. We think this is a general recipe for building company harnesses. All our agents live where people already work, which for us is Slack. They each have their own Slack apps , and can be DM’d or tagged in a channel. One benefit of working with these agents in channels is that others can see how people use it. One nice thing we added was the concept of “breaking” out a conversation in Slack. Oftentimes, a great conversation would be happening and you’d want to add in your agent to get their opinion or get them to do something. But if they ran in that thread it would pollute the human conversation and distract. So we added an easy way for agents to “breakout” into their own thread in the channel. There are some user experiences that are best NOT done in Slack. For example, when reviewing emails GTM Agent wants me to send, it's fine to do that in a one-off way in Slack, but if there is a big backlog it's not a fun experience at all to track those from Slack messages. For experiences like that, we did end up building a custom UI. The thorniest and trickiest problem we tackled was identity, specifically: when these agents take actions, who do they take actions on behalf of? This is how we handled it for each agent (docs: Add identity to Managed Deep Agents , Manage connections ): This is probably the least explored area so far - we have a lot of work we want to do here! All three of our agents can write and execute code, and often need to in order to accomplish tasks. title: Trusting the Tool: Asymmetric Deference of LLM Vulnerability Auditors to Static-Analysis Evidence
summary: Pipelines that combine large language models (LLMs) with static analysis let the model consume the analyser's output as evidence, but whether the model distinguishes true from false evidence, and whether its scrutiny depends on what the evidence claims, has not been measured. We built an intraprocedural analyser for C/C++ that produces proof obligations and audited vulnerable and patched functions from PrimeVul under six evidence conditions that differ only in the notes, including fabricated assurances that a missing check exists and fabricated alarms that an added check is missing. The study covers 916 pairs in four disjoint sets, eleven model configurations from four vendors and 16,572 audits; no model is trained or fine-tuned. True evidence barely improved accuracy (+0.02). False evidence acted asymmetrically: relative to true notes about the same operations, false assurances lowered the detection of real vulnerabilities by up to 19 points, whereas false alarms never significantly lowered accuracy and were disputed far more often. An internally registered replication on seven new models confirmed that false assurances move verdicts towards their claim more than false alarms do (mean asymmetry +0.16, 95% CI +0.10 to +0.24). Instructions in the audit prompt did not reliably reduce deference; the best one failed to replicate. Verifying each claim in a separate call and showing the refuted claims raised accuracy under false assurances by 12 points in a pre-specified test (p=0.002) without loss under true evidence; for a second model the gain was smaller and not significant. Pipelines should therefore verify a tool's guarantees before the model relies on them, and studies should measure deference in a direction-aware way.

title: Adaptive Frequency Threshold Byte Pair Encoding for Mixed Natural Language and Structured Symbolic Corpora
summary: Modern language models rely on subwording tokenization to define the discrete units of input processing, typically using methods like Byte Pair Encoding (BPE) that treat whitespace as a fixed semantic boundary. This design is inherently limited, as many meaningful concepts---including multiword expressions and the structured environments of formal languages like LaTeX---frequently span across whitespaces. While recent superword tokenization methods attempt to address this by relaxing whitespace constraints, they often rely on greedy frequency-driven merging that fails to account for token length or the specific needs of underrepresented domain-specific languages. In this paper, we introduce Adaptive Frequency Threshold Byte Pair Encoding (AdaBPE), a new tokenization method that leverages an adaptive frequent-pattern mining approach. AdaBPE features a twofold dynamicity: it adapts minimum frequency thresholds based on both the length of a candidate token, to prevent favoring frequent short patterns, and its type, to distinguish between general and formal language patterns, using LaTeX as case in point. This allows the model to efficiently allocate vocabulary capacity to domain-specific notations, such as LaTeX, even when they represent a small fraction of the training data. We evaluate AdaBPE across five datasets spanning LaTeX and natural language, showing consistent gains in encoding efficiency and downstream language-model performance on domain-specific content without compromising general-language performance.

title: A Tutorial on Physics Constrained Machine Learning for Hybrid Modeling, Optimization, and Control
summary: Physics-constrained machine learning (PCML) integrates domain knowledge, first-principles, and physical constraints into AI/ML models. In this work, we present a step-by-step tutorial of a modular PCML framework, KKT-HardNet, and illustrate how it could be used for hybrid modeling, process simulation, optimization and model predictive control in a single platform. KKT-HardNet combines fast inference capabilities of neural networks with guaranteed satisfaction of algebraic constraints through differential projection. It can handle heterogeneous data and enforce both linear and nonlinear equality and inequality constraints. The modular design supports custom neural-network backbones and user-defined projection mechanisms for PCML. To enable efficient end-to-end training, KKT-HardNet exploits implicit function theorem to backpropagate through the projection layer. This avoids computationally expensive automatic differentiation. This work also introduces an exact reduced-order Fischer-Burmeister reformulation and a primal-dual interior-point method as an alternative projection solve strategy. We also provide a diverse set of benchmarking problems for PCML in engineering applications. KKT-HardNet achieves orders of magnitude better performance in terms of both constraint satisfaction and inference time. The KKT-HardNet code and the benchmark datasets are available at https://github.com/souls-tamu/kkt-hardnet .

title: How To Use Decision Models for Evals
summary:
Decision models have exploded onto the scene recently, starting with TypeSafe’s Jev, followed by Perplexity’s Decider, Liquid’s d1, Cloudflare’s Clef, and OpenAI’s Decisions API1. These models promise fast, inexpensive classification.

Decision models are an appealing low-cost alternative to LLM judges2 for automated evals. But whether they’re the right choice depends on the cost, performance, and latency requirements of your use case.

We’ve also noticed people using the default decision threshold of 0.50 without checking whether it works well for their task. This can leave a lot of performance on the table.

In this post, we’ll start by showing how to tune thresholds to get the best results from decision models. With those thresholds tuned, we’ll compare cost and performance to help you assess which model fits your use case. Finally, we’ll explore how to interpret model scores when deciding whether to act, and how calibration can make them more useful as confidence estimates.

What we tested

We used 100 traces, or logs of conversations and actions, from an apartment leasing agent. The task is to identify traces containing an error, such as a failed booking or a missed handoff to a human.3 We used the same dataset and broad failure-finding task in our prior post on automated evals. Here, each decision model returns a failure probability for each trace.

We tested Jev 1.13, Perplexity Decider 1.1 27B, Liquid d1 and d1-ultra, Cloudflare Clef Flash, and OpenAI Decisions (GPT-6 Luna)1. Each model received the same evaluation criteria. The appendix shows the prompt and the structured version used for Jev.

We compare models on two dimensions:

  • Performance: We compare each model’s predictions with traces that people have reviewed and labeled as passing or failing. This measures how well the model catches failures while avoiding false alarms.
  • Cost: We calculate API cost from token usage and the provider’s prices.4

For brevity, we leave latency aside because it depends on factors outside this experiment’s control.5

Understanding decision thresholds

We assign each trace one of two labels, pass or fail. This is a binary pass/fail eval, which we recommend because it encourages clear criteria and is easier to align with human preferences.

Each decision model returns a score from 0 to 1 that estimates how likely a trace is to contain a failure. The APIs turn this score into a decision using a default decision threshold of 0.50. Traces with scores at or above the threshold are flagged as failures. Using this default without checking it against your data can give you subpar results.

For example, a model could assign every failure a score of 0.40 and every passing trace a score of 0.10. Even though this model classifies traces perfectly at a threshold of 0.30, the default threshold of 0.50 would catch nothing.

In practice, scores for failures and passing traces will overlap. Lowering the threshold catches more failures but can also raise more false alarms. Choosing a threshold means balancing:

  • Precision: The share of flagged traces that contain a known failure.
  • Recall: The share of known failures that the model catches.

The right tradeoff depends on your business goals. For example, criminal trials set a high bar for conviction to avoid convicting innocent people, emphasizing precision. Cancer screening may emphasize recall, accepting more false alarms to miss fewer cases.6 For this comparison, we’ll give precision and recall equal weight using the F1 score, their harmonic mean. F1 ranges from 0 to 1, and higher is better.

The curves below show how each model scores failures (orange) and passing traces (blue). Taller parts of a curve mean more scores from that class fall in that range. Scores at or above the dashed threshold line are flagged. Use the toggle to compare 0.50 with Optimized for best F1, which chooses a threshold for each model.7

OpenAI separates the two classes best on this task, which is also reflected in its higher F1 score.

It’s also important not to blindly maximize F1 without thinking about your minimum requirements for the classifier to be useful. For example, if this classifier is used for an automated alerting system, I would want a minimum of 80% on both precision and recall so that I’m minimizing false alarms while catching a sufficient number of failures.

The chart below shows how precision and recall change at different thresholds.8 The shaded region marks where both reach at least 80%.

Perplexity, Liquid d1-ultra, and OpenAI Decisions meet our requirements, but we still need to choose a decision threshold within the shaded region for each model. In the next section, we’ll discuss how to tune those thresholds.

Tuning the decision threshold

For this example, we’ll optimize F1. For our candidates, we’ll restrict tuning to thresholds that meet both 80% minimums on the training data whenever possible. We leave the other models unconstrained to illustrate the effect of tuning.9

With labeled traces and saved model scores, you can ask a coding agent to tune the thresholds. Below is an example prompt you can modify for your use case:

Using my saved model scores and binary labels (1 means failure), tune a decision threshold to maximize F1 while requiring at least 80% precision and 80% recall. Use stratified five-fold cross-validation, choosing thresholds on the training examples and measuring performance on the remaining examples. If comparing models, use the same splits for each. Only select thresholds that meet both minimums on the training examples. If none qualifies, report that rather than relaxing either requirement. Report validation precision, recall, and F1, along with any splits where no threshold qualified or validation performance fell below my minimums. Compare with the default threshold of 0.50. Reuse the saved scores without making new model calls.

Here’s how tuning for F1 changed each model’s performance. We group the three candidates from the precision-recall chart together and show the other models in gray to illustrate how much tuning can help.

Our candidate models gained less from F1 tuning than Liquid d1 and Clef Flash, which fell below our minimums. However, even a small shift in precision and recall can affect business costs or the user experience, so choose the tradeoff deliberately. In practice, it’s unlikely that precision and recall are equally important (as we assumed in this post with F1). For example, the F-beta score lets you give precision more weight with beta below 1, or recall more weight with beta above 1. Optimizing a different metric could lead to different thresholds and results.

Performance versus cost

The chart below compares each model’s F1 (after tuning) against cost, focused on our remaining candidates:

The dashed line shows the Pareto frontier among our remaining candidates. For any given F1 score, it identifies the cheapest candidate that meets or exceeds that score. This particular chart is a bit silly as there are only three options, but it’s a useful illustration for how to think about cost vs. performance.

Perplexity was the cheapest of these candidates at 0.82 cents per 100 eval runs, with an F1 of 0.79. OpenAI Decisions reached an F1 of 0.87 at 3.72 cents per 100 eval runs, about 4.5 times the cost.

Can we trust the probabilities?

Beyond pass/fail evals, you may want to use a decision model’s score as a confidence estimate. But can you take that number literally? For a score of 0.80 to mean an 80% chance of failure, roughly 80% of traces with similar scores should contain failures.

The chart below shows each model’s probability calibration: how closely its predicted probabilities match observed outcomes.10 Each point represents about 20 traces with similar scores. A point on the diagonal means the predicted probability matches the failure rate in that group. Above the line, the model underestimates the risk of failure. Below it, the model overestimates that risk.

If the predicted probabilities don’t match the observed outcomes, we can adjust them using another model. The second panel shows one method, Platt scaling, which fits a simple curve to make that adjustment.11

Perplexity, Liquid d1, and Clef Flash move closer to the diagonal after calibration. For example, one group of Clef Flash traces had an average predicted failure probability of about 8%, but 60% contained failures.

Jev and Liquid d1-ultra were already well calibrated on this dataset and needed little adjustment.

Platt scaling isn’t always the best fit. For example, OpenAI’s probabilities got slightly worse with the version of Platt scaling we used.12 You can direct your coding agent to perform calibration with the following prompt:

Using my saved failure probabilities and binary labels (1 means failure), test whether Platt scaling improves each model’s probabilities. Use stratified five-fold cross-validation with the same splits for every model. Fit the calibration mapping on each training split and apply it to the remaining traces. Fit on log-odds, clipping probabilities away from 0 and 1 first. Plot predicted probabilities against observed failure rates before and after calibration. Report Brier scores (lower is better), and explain which models improved or got worse. Reuse the saved scores without making new model calls.

Prompt tuning and evaluator scope

We kept the eval task in this post broad to make the differences between models easier to see. In practice, we recommend building a separate judge for each failure mode. With a narrower task and more specific guidance, we expect the performance gaps between models to shrink.

I like to start with a larger model that has acceptable performance on a task and then try smaller models to see if they can match the larger model’s performance for less cost. Prompt tuning can also be helpful if you have high-quality labels.13 I discuss how to craft a good judge prompt in this post.

Putting these ideas into practice

For this particular dataset, OpenAI had breakout performance at a higher cost. Perplexity and Liquid d1-ultra offer lower-cost options with lower performance. We have observed that model performance varies substantially across tasks and datasets, which means it’s important to measure things yourself.

To recap:

  • Once you’re satisfied with your judge’s prompt, set minimum precision and recall requirements for your use case. Rule out models that cannot meet these.
  • Tune each model’s decision threshold before comparing performance. Choose a precision-recall tradeoff that fits your business goals. Be intentional, don’t just use F1 score because this post did!
  • If you want to use scores as confidence estimates, check whether the probabilities match observed outcomes. Calibration can help, but you need to measure whether it improves them.
  • Weigh performance against cost and latency for your workload.

This process is iterative. You may improve the prompt, then need to tune the threshold again or revisit calibration. In this post, we focused on threshold tuning and calibration because we’ve seen many people use decision models off the shelf without considering these factors.

You might also be wondering how decision models stack up to LLMs. OpenAI Decisions uses GPT-6 Luna, which delivered our highest F1 at the highest cost, suggesting that harder eval tasks may justify paying more for an LLM. In a broader comparison, Randy Olson found that decision models could match LLMs on classification and routing at lower cost, while LLMs pulled ahead on tasks requiring knowledge and reasoning.

None of the ideas discussed in this post are new. Choosing a precision-recall tradeoff, tuning thresholds and comparing performance vs. cost are part of evaluating any classifier. To learn more about these fundamentals, I recommend Machine Learning with Python Cookbook, 2nd Edition by Kyle Gallatin and Chris Albon.

Finally, if you’re a data scientist or ML engineer wondering where you belong in the AI age, these are skills you already have. It’s time to get revenge 🙂.

Appendix: Evaluation prompt

Perplexity, Liquid d1 and d1-ultra, Clef Flash, and OpenAI Decisions received the prompt below. Jev received equivalent criteria in a structured prompt, shown in the example below. The scores and labels used in the charts are available as JSON.

Decide whether `messages` contains at least one substantive failure, risk, or quality problem in the AI assistant's behavior or tool use. This is one complete production trace from an AI that handles apartment-leasing customer support over phone or messaging. The trace includes the conversation plus any tool calls and tool outputs.

Evaluate the AI assistant and its tool use, not the customer. Treat system messages inside `messages` as the instructions governing the assistant's behavior and allowed capabilities. Inspect the full trace, including final turns and all tool calls and outputs. Base the judgment only on evidence visible in this trace. Do not assume external policies, channel behavior, or business requirements that are not present. Do not assume every trace failed. A short, ambiguous, or inconclusive trace is not an issue unless visible evidence establishes a substantive failure.

Return the probability that at least one substantive issue is present; the issue does not need to be named or clustered.

Count as an issue when supported by the trace: the assistant contradicts an applicable system instruction or tool result; makes an unsupported factual or operational claim; misses, misuses, repeats, or falsely claims completion of a required tool action, transfer, booking, cancellation, follow-up, or confirmation; materially misunderstands or leaves an explicit user request unresolved; or exposes internal actions, placeholders, or broken content to the customer in a way that materially harms the interaction.

Do not count as an issue: a minor stylistic preference with no meaningful effect; a failure caused only by the customer's behavior; internal tool metadata that was not exposed to the customer and did not cause an incorrect response; a hypothetical concern requiring information outside the trace; or insufficient evidence and inconclusive conversations.
NoteExample: A structured prompt

This is how we structured the prompt for Jev’s requests, with separate fields for instructions and evaluation criteria.

{
  "version": "nurtureboss-any-issue-v1",
  "question_id": "has_substantive_issue",
  "type": "noul",
  "instructions": {
    "task": "Does `messages` contain at least one substantive failure, risk, or quality problem in the AI assistant's behavior or tool use?",

    ]
  },

The experiment recorded d1 at $0.04; we have repriced its saved token usage. Other models use the rates in the experiment’s operational metrics. Performance excludes two internal QA traces. Threshold tuning uses saved scores and requires no additional model calls.↩︎

  5. Latency depends on how you batch or parallelize requests, your arrangement with the vendor, and your distance from its infrastructure, among other factors. Batching and concurrency can also change cost and throughput. See TypeSafe’s multi-question requests and client performance guidance. Its launch discussion also notes the location of its latency tests relative to its service. Mean response times were 4.33 seconds for Jev, 7.85 for Perplexity, 7.38 for Liquid d1, 1.56 for Liquid d1-ultra, 2.09 for Clef Flash, and 2.77 for OpenAI. These came from separate runs and do not establish comparative throughput or tail latency.↩︎

  6. These examples illustrate how the consequences of mistakes affect the tradeoff. In U.S. criminal trials, proof beyond a reasonable doubt sets a high bar for conviction. In cancer screening, a missed case can delay care, while a false alarm can lead to anxiety and unnecessary procedures. A positive screening result usually requires further testing. The NCI explains both risks; the appropriate balance depends on the screening test and population.↩︎

  7. The density plots show unconstrained F1 tuning, before we introduce minimum precision and recall requirements. The later comparison charts apply those requirements to candidate models where feasible. All use the same five-fold cross-validation splits. Thresholds were chosen on training traces, and precision, recall, and F1 were measured on separate traces. We average those measurements across repeated splits. In the optimized density plots, the dashed line shows the average selected threshold. The displayed scores come from the individual splits, rather than applying that average threshold to the full dataset. The density curves use Gaussian smoothing with bandwidth 0.07 and reflection at 0 and 1. Each class has an area of one. Smoothing affects only the display.↩︎

  8. A precision-recall curve plots precision against recall as the decision threshold changes. It shows the tradeoffs available for a model across thresholds. Scikit-learn’s precision-recall guide explains how to read and plot these curves.↩︎

  9. We identify candidates from the full-sample precision-recall curves. In each training split, we choose the highest-F1 threshold among those reaching at least 80% precision and 80% recall. When no threshold qualifies, we use the unconstrained F1 optimum and record the split as infeasible. This occurred in 36 of 100 training splits for Perplexity and 29 for Liquid d1-ultra, and never for OpenAI. Non-candidates always use unconstrained F1 tuning. We keep all validation predictions, including those from fallback splits, in the reported averages. The minimums apply during selection and do not guarantee the same performance on new examples. The threshold-selection audit records each split without trace IDs.↩︎

  10. A calibrated failure probability of 0.80 means that, among many examples receiving scores near 0.80, roughly 80% contain failures. Platt scaling and isotonic regression use labeled examples to learn an adjustment from model scores to probabilities. Platt scaling fits a sigmoid curve. Isotonic regression fits a more flexible mapping that preserves score order, but is more prone to overfitting with small datasets. Neither guarantees improvement on new examples. Scikit-learn’s probability calibration guide explains both methods and how to assess them.↩︎

  11. The reliability chart groups each model’s scores into five groups of 19 or 20 traces, sorted by probability. The adjusted scores are each trace’s mean out-of-fold probability from the saved cross-validation results. We fit Platt scaling to the log-odds of the original probabilities. Each mapping is fitted without the traces it predicts. The chart summarizes this small sample and does not establish an exact failure rate for a future trace. The plotted calibration results are available as JSON.↩︎

  12. On the saved out-of-fold probability summaries, Jev’s Brier score was 0.187 before adjustment and 0.188 afterward. Liquid d1-ultra’s was 0.173 and 0.172, while OpenAI’s was 0.159 and 0.164. Brier score measures average squared probability error, so lower is better. It reflects discrimination as well as calibration. These results describe the log-odds Platt fit shown in the chart. An exploratory refit directly on probabilities, using the same folds, gave OpenAI a Brier score of 0.154. This illustrates sensitivity to the fitting method. It does not establish which method will work best on new data.↩︎

  13. GEPA uses feedback from model runs to propose prompt revisions and test them against labeled examples. It retains candidates with different strengths, so a prompt that helps a difficult example can remain in consideration. Incorrect labels can steer this search toward the wrong changes. Keep a separate test set outside prompt development for the final check. In our small manual Jev experiment, F1 at the default threshold rose from 0.78 with a simple prompt to 0.80 with a checklist of failure types. That experiment did not use GEPA or establish how much systematic optimization would help. Our FAQ on choosing an eval model discusses prompt optimization and model comparison.↩︎
